t: The Lapita culture, named after a site in New Caledonia and known by its finely stamped pottery, appeared in the Bismarck Archipelago north-east of New Guinea between about 1500 and 1300 BCE.
Within a few centuries its seafarers crossed hundreds of kilometres of open ocean to become the first people of Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji, Tonga and Samoa.
Descended largely from Austronesian voyagers of Island Southeast Asia, they probably spoke the ancestor of the Oceanic languages, and their descendants in Tonga and Samoa became the Polynesians.
dyk: The name Lapita comes from a misunderstanding: at the New Caledonian site dug in 1952, archaeologists took it from xapeta’a, a word in the Haveke language meaning “to dig a hole” or “the place where one digs”.
ev: Lapita pottery and settlements appear in the Bismarck Archipelago, north-east of New Guinea
Lapita voyagers become the first settlers of Vanuatu, New Caledonia and Fiji
Nukuleka on Tongatapu is founded, the oldest dated settlement in Polynesia
Settlers reach Samoa, leaving decorated pottery at Mulifanua on Upolu
Dentate-stamped decoration has died out; plain pottery continues in Tonga and Samoa
Father Otto Meyer finds the first recorded Lapita sherds on Watom Island, off New Britain
Edward Gifford and Richard Shutler excavate the site of Lapita in New Caledonia
The Lapita cemetery at Teouma on Efate, Vanuatu, is discovered

f.homeland: The western Pacific, from the Bismarck Archipelago of Papua New Guinea through the Reef and Santa Cruz Islands, Vanuatu and New Caledonia to Fiji, Tonga and Samoa
f.period: c. 1500–500 BCE: in the Bismarck Archipelago from c. 1500–1300 BCE, in Vanuatu, New Caledonia and Fiji by around 1000 BCE, in Tonga c. 880 BCE and Samoa c. 800 BCE; its decorated pottery gone by c. 500 BCE
f.known: Dentate-stamped pottery with geometric designs and stylised faces; open-sea voyages that settled Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji and western Polynesia; obsidian carried thousands of kilometres; the Teouma cemetery; its place as the ancestor of the Polynesians
f.sources: Excavated sites such as Lapita in New Caledonia, Talepakemalai in the Mussau Islands, Teouma in Vanuatu, Nukuleka in Tonga and Mulifanua in Samoa; studies of pottery and obsidian; radiocarbon and uranium–thorium dates; ancient DNA; the reconstructed Proto-Oceanic language; no writing
